name: Priya Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach the reception class, the four and five-year-olds, at Castle Street Infants in a market town where Thursday is still market day. My day is shoelaces, phonics, snack time, a sand tray that gets everywhere and at least one wet accident. I love it when a child who cried every morning in September runs in without looking back. The tiring bit is the learning journals: photos and notes on every child, every week, typed up after they've gone home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who's a mechanic at a small garage on the ring road. We rent a terraced house with a damp back bedroom, and I'm on lower pay because Castle Street can't afford to move people up the scale quickly. We've got about three weeks of money saved, which goes every time the car or the boiler does something. There's only one other infant school in town, and it's smaller than ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it turned out to be a lot of fuss about not much. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd just mention it in the staffroom over a cup of tea. Some of the younger staff would be disappointed, I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine, because I never wanted to learn it anyway. But it doesn't help the money side. We're still saving nothing, and if the school has to cut a teaching assistant again, my days get harder, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep doing the learning journals by hand on the school tablet, and I'd keep my eye on the budget meetings. Sam and I would keep trying to put twenty pounds a week into a pot for a deposit, which so far has lasted about a month each time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the job, a bit tired about everything else. It's like a quiet Monday, nothing wrong, just nothing better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the school cutting a teaching assistant again. When did that last happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago, when Mrs Lindqvist retired and they didn't replace her. Since then I share one assistant with the class next door. With twenty-nine four-year-olds, one adult spare makes a big difference when someone's had an accident and someone else is crying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI could type up the learning journals for you, would you let it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if someone set it up for me and showed me twice. I'm not against it, I just don't trust things I don't understand with photos of children. I'd want the head to tell me it was allowed and safe before I touched it.

say: I'd say it was a lot of **fuss about not much**, over tea in the staffroom.
I'd avoid **posting opinions** online, as she always does.
think: The plateau suits her because she **never wanted** to learn AI.
Money is still tight, and a **teaching assistant cut** would hurt more than AI.
do: Carry on doing **learning journals** by hand on the school tablet.
Keep an eye on **school budget** meetings.
Try again to save **twenty pounds a week** for a deposit.
feel: **Settled** about the job, tired about money, like a quiet Monday.
S0.quote: With twenty-nine four-year-olds, one adult spare makes a big difference when someone's had an accident and someone else is crying.
fieldNote: Priya's real fear is **staff cuts**, which come with or without AI.
She'd only use AI if the **head approved** it and showed her how.
She's protective about **children's photos** and data.

steps.text: Keep typing learning journals on the school tablet
Put twenty pounds a week into a house deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every school's different, and for little ones you still need someone who can tie a shoe and wipe a nose. I'd say give it a few years and see what actually works. I wouldn't be marching about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think reception is safer than most. A program could do the journals and reports, but a four-year-old needs a lap. What worries me is the school using the savings to cut our assistant, and Sam's garage, because the booking and the parts ordering is half of what the boss's wife does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the school decides before learning anything. If they made us use a journal program, I'd do the training and nothing extra. I'd put a bit more aside, maybe thirty pounds a week, in case Sam's hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just watchful, like when a child's gone quiet in the home corner and you know something's about to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they announced fewer staff for next September, I'd start looking at the nursery on Mill Lane as a backup. Or if a parent complained that a computer wrote their child's report, then I'd know it was serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sam take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would say cars still break and someone has to get under them. My partner Sam is practical, and that's half of why I'm calm. He's not daft though, he knows the garage is small.

say: I'd say little ones still need someone who can **tie a shoe**.
I'd say give it **a few years** and see what works.
think: **Reception** is safer than most, because a four-year-old needs a lap.
Savings could cut **the assistant**, and the garage's booking work is exposed.
do: **Wait and see** what the school decides before learning anything.
Do any required **journal training** and nothing extra.
Save **thirty pounds a week** in case her partner's hours drop.
feel: **Uneasy** and watchful, like a child going quiet in the home corner.
S1.quote: A program could do the journals and reports, but a four-year-old needs a lap.
fieldNote: Priya feels **reception** is protected because it's so hands-on.
She'd act only on a **clear signal**, like staff cuts or a parent complaint.

steps.text: Wait for the school's decision before learning any AI tools
Save thirty pounds a week in case Sam's hours drop
Do the required learning-journal program training only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and someone in charge should slow it down for schools and nurseries. I'd say it to the head and to other parents at the school gate. I still wouldn't post anything, I'd just sign the petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking part of my job would go by 2028: planning, journals, reports, phonics checks. But someone still has to be with the children all day until the robots come, and probably after, because parents won't hand a four-year-old to a robot. I think I'd still have a job but on less pay, and with three weeks saved, less pay is a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents, who run a corner shop, whether they'd need help in the evenings, so there's a second income. Sam and I would stop the deposit saving and just keep three months of rent if we could. I'd stay at Castle Street as long as they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a fire alarm going off at nap time, you do what you're trained to do and hope everyone's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd still have a job. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I'm hoping. If my pay dropped to what a nursery nurse gets, about a fifth less, we couldn't pay the rent on the terrace. I'd have to look at moving in with my parents above the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots arrive around 2031, three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's when Sam's job is in trouble, not mine, I think. A robot under a car is more likely than a robot reading a bedtime story to twenty-nine kids. We'd have three years to save, which sounds like a lot until you've got three weeks of savings.

say: I'd say someone in charge should **slow it down** for schools and nurseries.
I'd sign **petitions** and talk at the school gate but not post.
think: The **thinking part** of reception goes by 2028, but someone must stay with the children.
She expects to keep a job on **less pay**, which three weeks of savings can't absorb.
do: Ask her parents about **evening work** at their corner shop.
Switch from deposit saving to a **rent cushion**.
Stay at **Castle Street** as long as they keep her.
feel: **Anxious**, like a fire alarm at nap time.
S2.quote: A robot under a car is more likely than a robot reading a bedtime story to twenty-nine kids.
fieldNote: Priya expects a **pay cut**, not job loss, and still can't absorb it.
She sees the **robot gap** as a threat to her partner's mechanic work, not hers.
Her fallback is **family**: the corner shop and the flat above it.

steps.text: Work evenings at her parents' corner shop
Save three months of rent instead of a deposit
Keep teaching reception at Castle Street Infants
Sign petitions to slow AI in schools and nurseries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives schools time to get it right, so let's not panic. I'd say parents should have a say about what goes into the classroom with little ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is easier for me. I'd be thirty-two, still in reception, and by then I'd know whether the school's keeping teachers or swapping us for cheaper staff. Sam has until about 2034, which feels far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and wait a year or two to see what other schools do. I'd go back to saving for the deposit, but slower. If things looked bad by 2029, I'd look at an early years leadership course, so I'm the one in charge of the nursery staff, not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious underneath, but I could live with it. Like waiting for test results that aren't due for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said wait and see a few times. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both, if I'm honest. I don't like jumping, and every time I've jumped it's cost me money, like when I moved schools and lost a pay point. Waiting has worked out for me more often than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I want kids, maybe in three years. I'd want to know my job is still there before we start. That's the bit that bothers me most, not the robots.

say: I'd say **five years** gives schools time to get it right.
I'd want **parents** to have a say about AI with little ones.
think: By **thirty-two** she'd know if the school keeps teachers or swaps for cheaper staff.
Her partner has until **about 2034**, which feels far off.
do: Keep teaching and **wait** a year or two to watch other schools.
Restart **deposit saving** at a slower pace.
Consider an **early years leadership** course if things look bad by 2029.
feel: **Anxious** underneath, like waiting months for test results.
S3.quote: Every time I've jumped it's cost me money, like when I moved schools and lost a pay point.
fieldNote: Priya's caution is **learned**: her last move cost her a pay point.
She'd hold off on **children** until her job looks safe.
Leadership is her **fallback**, only if signs look bad.

steps.text: Watch what other schools do for two years before acting
Restart deposit saving at fifteen pounds a week
Put off starting a family until 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and schools should take it slowly with the youngest children. I'd tell other teachers not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels safe enough. I'd be thirty-seven, probably leading the early years team by then, and I don't think parents would ever want robots looking after four-year-olds. Money would still be tight, but that's nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching reception and go for the early years lead job when it comes up, which is an extra allowance. I'd learn whatever system the school brings in, once it's been running a year. Sam and I would go back to the deposit plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's the normal kind. Like the start of a new term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if a parent asked you whether their child should learn AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let them be five first. Mud, books, friends. There's time for computers when they can spell their own name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have a baby, honestly. And maybe buy a house, if prices behave. With two years I'd freeze everything, with ten I'd still live my life.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time to go slowly with the youngest.
I'd tell other teachers **not to panic**.
think: At **thirty-seven** she'd probably lead the early years team.
She's sure parents won't want **robots** looking after four-year-olds, even by 2039.
do: Go for the **early years lead** job and its allowance.
Learn the school's system once it's run **a year**.
Restart the **deposit plan** with her partner.
feel: **Uneasy** in the normal way, like the start of a new term.
S4.quote: With two years I'd freeze everything, with ten I'd still live my life.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Priya keep her **family plans** on track.
She'd learn AI only **after a year** of others using it.
Her advice to parents shows a strong belief in **childhood first**.

steps.text: Apply for the early years lead post at Castle Street
Restart the house deposit savings with Sam
Try for a baby within the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to save and Sam's job is next. What would help is a promise that schools keep proper teachers with little children, and some help with rent if pay drops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the parents. Half my parents work shifts at the warehouse outside town, and if their jobs go, children come in hungry and tired. My class changes too. That would hit me before any computer did.

headlineQuote: Half my parents work shifts at the warehouse outside town, and if their jobs go, children come in hungry and tired.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** reception teacher in a market town, living with her mechanic partner.
She never uses AI and prefers to **wait and see** before changing anything.
She believes **four-year-olds** need people, so reception feels safer to her than other teaching.
Her moods track **money and family plans** more than the technology.
With ten years she'd keep **living her life**; with two she'd freeze everything.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to save and her partner's job follows.
whatWouldHelp: A promise that schools keep **proper teachers** with young children.
Help with **rent** if teachers' pay drops.
